column2: My toys were stacked in a perfect tower this morning, though I never touched a single block. The nurses whisper when they think I cannot hear. Mother laughs a little too loudly, and does not meet my eyes.

Stray cat-owls, a lost turtle-duck, even the headman's surly hog-monkey: every beast in the village trails after me, as if they had known me all their lives. I share my supper with all of them, and they let me.
The fever should have taken me. The healer said as much, quietly, to my parents. Then the wind changed in the night, the shutters banged, and by dawn I sat up asking for breakfast.
I am simply hard to kill
No one taught me a single form, yet the washbasin emptied itself across the courtyard in a perfect arc, twice. I insist I did nothing. The puddles suggest otherwise.
Such things are not for me
I dream of a city of walls within walls, and a throne room I have never entered, in perfect detail. This morning I wept for a friend with yellow eyes. I have never left the valley.
I will draw it before it fades
Three older children had the miller's boy cornered behind the grain store. I have two black eyes now, and the miller's boy has a protector who shares his lunch without being asked.
I will always stand my ground
I will protect the small and weak

Travellers in faded blue, sages by their manners, asked me odd questions about my birthmarks, and the storms on the night I was born, and whether the candles ever lean toward me. They left gifts and took nothing.
When the cart overturned and pinned my friend, my eyes shone, truly shone, and the cart moved. No one speaks of it directly. Everyone speaks of nothing else.
I must learn stillness, and control
I am afraid of what lives inside me
Down by the water, something old spoke to me of balance, and of a bridge between worlds that has gone untended. I came home barefoot and glowing, and refused to say where I had been.
I will devote myself to the spirits
I will share the blessing around

I woke before dawn and my crib was warm as a hearth, though the fire had died hours before. Mother pressed her hand to my brow, found nothing amiss, and stayed anyway, watching me the way she watches storms on the horizon.
I am not afraid of the dark

I took my first true steps today, and every loose leaf in the courtyard rose to walk beside me. The grown-ups laughed and clapped. I did not yet understand why they went quiet when they thought I was not looking.

I dreamed of a sky on fire and a thousand voices crying out for water. I woke the whole house screaming and could not tell them why, only that somewhere, someone I loved was dying and I could not reach them.
The cat-owl's wing was broken and I held it until it stopped shivering. By morning it flew from my windowsill as though nothing had happened. Grandmother called it luck, and would not meet my eyes.

The tutor set down his brush and asked how I had learned to read the old script. I told him the truth: that I see it in my sleep. He did not set my lessons again for a week, and when he did, his hands shook.
I will study all the harder
I will say less of it
A boulder sat across the path to the well, taller than me. I rolled it aside without thinking, the way you move a chair. The other children stared. I told them I was hungry, and they let me pass.
I woke from a fever to find the room rearranged: every cup turned to face the water, every shutter open to the wind. The healer put them back before I could ask. She has not looked at me since.
The Note That Shook the Lanterns

At the festival I opened my mouth to sing and no song came, only one long note that set every lantern trembling on its hook. The crowd fell silent, and then the drums began, and they chose to forget me.

The travellers in faded blue came back, and this time they did not ask questions. They watched me cross the courtyard, and one of them, an old woman with a bad hip, bowed as I passed. I did not know what to do with my hands.

The village elder asked what I would be when I grew up: a farmer, a soldier, a wife or a husband, a nobody. I opened my mouth and heard myself say: I will keep the world in balance. The whole table laughed. I did not.

A boy from the next valley bested me at every game we played, and laughed about it, and I hated him for it. That night I dreamed I pushed him into the river and watched him sink. I woke sick with shame.
I will make peace with him

A cart came off the mountain road with a family inside, and I reached for it and it stopped in the air, stopped, and held, until they climbed free. Afterwards I could not lift my arms for three days. No one spoke of it. But they know now. I know they know.
I will deny it to the last
